label: Connectedness and Compactness
notes: Open the chapter, which spans printed pages 145 through 186. Connectedness and compactness are the two great topological properties preserved by continuous maps. We develop connected spaces and their behavior on the real line, then compact spaces, the Heine-Borel theorem, and the weaker notions of limit point and local compactness.

label: Connected Spaces
notes: A space is connected when it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open sets. The union of connected sets sharing a point is connected, and the continuous image of a connected space is connected. Path connectedness is a stronger companion notion that implies connectedness but, as the topologist's sine curve shows, is not equivalent.

label: Connected Subsets of the Line
notes: The connected subsets of the real line are exactly the intervals. From this the intermediate value theorem follows immediately: a continuous real-valued function on a connected domain takes every value between any two it attains. This recovers a familiar calculus theorem as a purely topological statement about connected images.

label: Compact Spaces
notes: A space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover. The continuous image of a compact space is compact, finite products of compact spaces are compact, and closed subsets of compact spaces are compact. Compactness in a Hausdorff space forces closedness, tightly coupling the two properties throughout analysis.

label: Compactness on the Line
notes: The Heine-Borel theorem identifies the compact subsets of Euclidean space as precisely the closed and bounded ones. As a consequence a continuous real-valued function on a compact space attains its maximum and minimum, the extreme value theorem, and is uniformly continuous on a compact metric domain.

label: Limit Point and Local Compactness
notes: Limit point compactness asks that every infinite subset have a limit point; in metric spaces it coincides with compactness and sequential compactness. Local compactness, where each point has a compact neighborhood, leads to the one-point compactification. These refinements prepare the separation and metrization theory of the next chapters.
